$comment: Single source of truth for the package versions every adopting repository
is held to. It names VERSIONS and never repositories: this repo has no
list of who consumes it, and should not -- a repository opts in by calling
job-ci-conformance, and the checker is handed one clone at a time.
IT WAS CALLED fleet-versions.json. The rename says what the file carries
instead of who it is aimed at, which is the half a reader could not
recover from the old name. `fleet` also implied a roster that does not
exist here and cannot: a handed-over client repository vendors this
standard and keeps using it after it leaves, and nothing in this tree
Nothing reads this at build time — each repo still declares its own pin in
the file its tooling actually reads (package.json packageManager,
package.json devDependencies, go.mod, .node-version), because that is what
corepack, pnpm, setup-go and setup-node consume both in CI and on a
developer's machine. This file is what those per-repo pins are checked
AGAINST: tools/check-dependency-versions compares every repo to the values
here, so drift is a failing check rather than something noticed months
later. Bumping a version here is the start of a wave, not the end: update
the value, then update every repo's own pin to match.
$packageManager_comment: Compared against package.json's `packageManager` field, which is what
corepack activates and what pnpm/action-setup reads in the shared jobs.
$devDependencies_comment: Compared against package.json's `devDependencies`, EXACTLY -- a caret or
tilde is a failure, not a near miss. A range is not a pin: two repos
declaring ^7.3.0 can resolve to different vite versions on different days,
which is the drift this file exists to stop.
ASSERTED WHERE PRESENT, as of wave 7. A unit that does not declare a
package below is not failed for it; a unit that declares it at another
version is. This paragraph used to say the opposite -- an entry had to be
carried by every repo or it did not belong here -- and that rule quietly
sealed the file shut. Measured across the nine Node units: ZERO
unasserted packages are present in all nine. Not one. So under the old
rule nothing could ever be added again, and a standard that cannot grow
is a description of the past.
What still enforces PRESENCE is the shared job that invokes the tool.
job-typecheck-ts-tsc runs `pnpm exec tsc`; a repo calling it without
typescript fails there, in the job whose name says what broke. Two
questions, two mechanisms: the catalog job decides whether you need the
tool, this file decides which version you get if you have it.
@types/node landed in wave 1 of aurum-alpha/workflows#169; the eslint six
landed in wave 2; the vite four landed in wave 3; typescript landed in
wave 5 and moved to its 7.x major in wave 6. All are converged across all
nine Node apps -- verified against each repo's main, not assumed -- which
is what makes them assertable now.
THE ESLINT SIX ARE NOW TWO, and the four that left were not dropped for
drifting -- they were removed from the portfolio. oxlint replaced eslint
outright: measured head-to-head on a real tree, every configured rule
matched finding for finding, including all seven that need a type checker,
and oxlint reported more besides. So eslint, @eslint/js,
eslint-config-prettier and typescript-eslint are gone.
oxlint and oxlint-tsgolint are asserted here as of this change. They were
held out while oxlint was mid-wave -- asserting a package before every repo
carries it fails the repos whose turn has not come, and a check expected to
fail is a check nobody reads. All nine Node apps now carry both at one
version, verified against each package.json rather than assumed.
They are NOT asserted as a provisional or watched entry. oxlint is the
portfolio's only JS linter and it is production software here: it has run
across every repo for releases, and against the portfolio eslint config it
matched every configured rule finding for finding, type-aware rules
included, and reported more besides. Callers are warn_only because the
repos do not pass yet -- roughly 870 errors and 3,700 warnings of existing
debt -- which is a fact about the code, not about the linter.
eslint-plugin-react-hooks and eslint-plugin-react-refresh STAY, and their
names are misleading about why: oxlint consumes both through its JS plugin
bridge, so they are oxlint dependencies now whatever their prefix says.
Removing them because they read as eslint packages would delete 14 of the
16 react-hooks rules the portfolio actually lints with.
typescript-eslint leaving is what unblocks TypeScript 7. It was the only
thing in the portfolio importing the typescript package as a LIBRARY, and TS 7
is the native Go port, whose default export is just version and
versionMajorMinor -- no createProgram, no TypeChecker. oxlint does not
care: oxlint-tsgolint ships its own typescript-go and has no dependency on
our pin at all. Do not add ts-node, ts-jest, typedoc, ts-morph or tsup --
each one re-imports that API and would re-pin the portfolio to TypeScript 6.
The React types join them here, and react/react-dom itself is asserted in
the `dependencies` block below. Until now this file could not say wave 4
had happened: the checker read devDependencies alone, react and react-dom
are runtime dependencies in all nine repos -- correctly -- and so were
invisible to it. Two changes closed that, in this order: jewelry-factory
moved @types/react out of `dependencies`, where it was the portfolio's only
one, and check-dependency-versions learned to read both sections. Both were
needed; either alone leaves React unassertable.
Wave 6 (typescript 7) HAS NOW RUN, and the entry below is 7.0.2. It was
blocked upstream once: no published typescript-eslint admitted TS 7 --
8.68.0, the latest at the time, still peered `>=4.8.4 <6.1.0` -- and that
peer is what capped this entry at 6.0.x. The cap went when the package
holding it left the portfolio, as the paragraph above says, and for a while
the entry stayed at 6.0.3 only because nobody had run the wave.
What the wave measured before moving, rather than after. 7.0.2 is npm's
`latest`, not a preview. Nothing in the portfolio peer-constrains typescript:
a sweep of every installed tree across all nine repos found exactly one
peer on the package, cosmiconfig 9.0.0 at `>=4.9.5`, marked optional --
unbounded above, so not a constraint at all. `tsc -b --noEmit --force`
passes on all nine, with --force so no .tsbuildinfo could fake it. The
rest of the pipeline is untouched by construction, and was checked
anyway: vite and esbuild strip types themselves and never load this
package, and a full run -- vite build, the esbuild server bundle, vitest
-- is green on both repo shapes, flight-watch for the root layout and
gofast's client/ for the subpackage one. It is also 4-6x faster:
hiring-tracker 10,984ms -> 2,230ms, event-manager 7,943 -> 1,957,
client-manager's client 2,935 -> 482.
One thing DOES break, knowingly. hiring-tracker's scripts/generate-erd.ts
imports the compiler API as a library, which TS 7 no longer ships: 2248
exports become 2. No gate catches it because scripts/ sits outside that
repo's tsconfig include, so the nine-repo sweep above never compiled it.
It is a documented developer command that will start failing with no CI
signal. Accepted rather than fixed, and tracked as
aurum-alpha/workflows#245 -- holding a portfolio compiler upgrade on one ERD
generator is the wrong trade. It is the ONLY exposure: that file is the
portfolio's only source import of `typescript`, and no repo declares ts-node,
ts-jest, typedoc, ts-morph, tsup, ts-patch or @microsoft/api-extractor.
On asserting a value before the repos carry it, which the rule at the top
of this block forbids. The standard_ref lag is what makes this safe, and
only for a MODIFICATION like this one. Callers read this file out of the
PINNED clone, so a repo still on the old pin asserts 6.0.3 and carries
6.0.3. A repo re-pinning bumps its typescript IN THE SAME COMMIT, so it
asserts 7.0.2 and carries 7.0.2. Neither state is red and there is no
window between them -- unlike wave A's REMOVAL, where repos had already
dropped what the older tree still demanded.
WAVE 8 IS THE FIRST TO USE THE WHERE-PRESENT RULE, and it adds seven:
esbuild, postcss, autoprefixer, tsx, concurrently and the two @types
packages. Not one of them is carried by all nine units -- they run from
five to seven -- so under the old all-or-nothing rule none could have been
written down at all. That rule is what wave 7 removed, and this is what it
was removed for.
EVERY TARGET WAS READ FROM pnpm-lock.yaml, NOT FROM THE MANIFESTS, and
that distinction is the whole finding. The ranges were not describing what
runs. concurrently was declared ^9.2.1 in six repos and all six were
installing 9.2.4. postcss was declared ^8.4.47 in one and ^8.5.3 in
another, both installing 8.5.26. Taking the declared floor as the target
would have pinned concurrently to 9.2.1 and DOWNGRADED six repos while
calling itself a no-op convergence.
autoprefixer is the case that shows why this needed doing at all. Six
units declared a ^10.4.x range off the same registry on the same day and
installed four different versions -- 10.4.20, 10.4.21, 10.5.2, 10.5.4 --
crossing a MINOR without anyone choosing to. That is not drift waiting to
happen; it had already happened and nothing could see it.
Targets are the version already resolved somewhere in the portfolio, never
npm latest: esbuild is 0.28.1 with 0.28.2 published, tsx is 4.22.4 with
4.23.13 published. Convergence and upgrade are different changes, and a
wave that does both cannot say which half broke. Dependabot proposes the
upgrades afterwards, one at a time, on their own evidence.
esbuild was the only real risk in the wave. 0.25 -> 0.28 crosses two
minors and esbuild is 0.x, where its own convention makes a minor bump
breaking. It landed as a catch-up rather than a migration: four of the six
repos already ran 0.28.1 through job-bundle-js-esbuild, and the two that
did not were proved by the image-starts job booting a container built from
the new bundle -- which is the check that matters, because a bundle that
compiles says nothing about a process that starts.
THE SCOPE IS THE DEV/BUILD LAYER. Compilers, bundlers, linters, test
runners, type packages: the toolchain that decides how a unit is built and
checked, which is the same question the shared jobs answer and therefore
the thing job-runner standardization actually needs. Runtime dependencies
-- the business-logic layer -- are OUT OF SCOPE for now, deliberately and
not for lack of candidates: @tanstack/react-query sits at one exact
version in eight of nine units and was drafted into wave 7 before being
pulled back out. Converging what an application depends on to do its job
is a different decision from converging what compiles it, it belongs to
the teams owning those applications, and it is not a prerequisite for
anything in the CI standard. The `dependencies` block below is what wave 4
landed; it is not an invitation to grow it.
The vite four are one entry in four lines, not four independent pins.
@vitejs/plugin-react peers vite ^8 only from 6.0.0, and vitest reaches vite
through @vitest/mocker, which admits vite 8 only from 4.1.0 -- so a repo
moving vite alone gets a SECOND vite in its tree rather than a moved one,
with no pnpm warning and a passing `vite build`. @vitest/coverage-v8 peers
an EXACT vitest version on top of that. Bump one of these here and the
other three move in the same wave, or the check passes on a tree that is
quietly wrong.
WAVE 9 IS drizzle-kit, AND IT IS THE CLI ONLY. drizzle-kit ran at five
versions across the six units that declare it -- 0.30.2, 0.30.6, 0.31.4
twice, 0.31.8, 0.31.10 -- and all six now carry 0.31.10, the current
stable latest, which expense-splitter already ran. 1.0.0 exists only as
rc.5 and was not a candidate.
drizzle-orm is NOT here and is not missing. It is the runtime library --
the one that ships -- so it belongs to the business-logic layer this block
holds out of scope. It happens to be converged at 0.45.2 across all six
already, which is worth knowing and is not a reason to assert it. Nor is
drizzle-zod, which genuinely drifts: 0.6.1, 0.7.0 in three, 0.7.1 in two.
Same layer, same answer, and the drift is left standing rather than fixed
by a wave that was scoped to the toolchain.
The failure mode this wave had to rule out is not a red build. drizzle-kit
GENERATES migration SQL, so a version change can alter committed output
that no test compares. Three units carry migration history -- credit-watch
with 2 files, jewelry-factory 2, hiring-tracker 14 against a 12-entry
journal -- and every snapshot in all three is format version 7,
postgresql. 0.30.x and 0.31.x both write version 7, so no format boundary
is crossed. `drizzle-kit check` was run before and after the bump in each
repo: it passed both times and rewrote nothing, leaving package.json and
pnpm-lock.yaml as the entire diff.
The two 0.30.x units move drizzle-kit's PRIVATE esbuild from 0.19.12 to
0.25.12, which looks alarming in a lockfile diff and is not. Their own
esbuild stays declared and resolved at the 0.28.1 asserted above; the
versions that move belong to the CLI's own tree and never touch the app
build.
WAVE 10 ASSERTS TWO AND REJECTS THREE, and the three rejections are what
the wave was actually worth. A survey of all nine Node units found five
packages already sitting at one exact version in every unit that declares
them -- convergence with nothing holding it, which is the cheapest thing
this file can lock down, because no repository has to change. Three of
the five turned out not to be convergence at all.
Asserted: @types/passport 1.0.17 (six units) and @types/pg 8.21.0
(three). Both are consumed: passport is a runtime dependency at 0.7.0 in
all six, pg is 8.x in all three, and the types track the same major.
eslint-plugin-import 2.31.0 (hiring-tracker, jewelry-factory) is NOT
here, because it is an orphan. eslint left the portfolio and this plugin did
not go with it. Neither repo's .oxlintrc.json names it: `plugins` is
[eslint, typescript, react] -- oxlint's own built-in rule sets, not npm
packages -- and `jsPlugins` loads exactly eslint-plugin-react-refresh and
eslint-plugin-react-hooks. No import/ rule is configured anywhere in
either tree. What the package still does is drag the deleted linter back
in: both lockfiles resolve it as
eslint-plugin-import@2.31.0(eslint@10.9.1(jiti@1.21.7)), so a plugin
nobody runs is the reason eslint 10.9.1 still installs. Asserting a
version would have written that down as the standard. It should be
deleted instead, along with hiring-tracker's eslint-plugin-react 7.37.5,
which is the same package in the same state.
@tailwindcss/vite 4.3.3 (four units) is the same shape with a different
smell. Only flight-watch imports it -- vite.config.ts, `tailwindcss()` in
the plugin list -- and only flight-watch runs tailwindcss 4.1.16.
credit-watch, expense-splitter and wardley-mapper declare the Tailwind v4
Vite plugin, run the v3 engine at 3.4.x, and build through
postcss.config.js, which never loads it. Four units agreeing on the
version of a package three of them do not use is not convergence, it is
one install command copied around.
@types/express 4.17.21 (six units) is held for a reason worth keeping
separate from the other two, because the package is genuinely used. The
types converged where the runtime did not: five units run express 4.21.2
or 4.22.2, hiring-tracker runs 5.1.0, and every one of them declares the
express 4 types. Asserting 4.17.21 would freeze a wrong-major types
package onto hiring-tracker and then fail the correct fix -- moving it to
@types/express 5 -- with no way to satisfy both. express itself is a
runtime dependency and out of scope by the rule above, so the types wait
on a decision about the express major rather than pre-empting it.
WAVE 11 IS THE FIRST WHERE PLACEMENT WAS THE ONLY BLOCKER, and it adds three.
@types/memoizee 0.4.12 (two units), @replit/vite-plugin-shadcn-theme-json
0.0.4 (two units) and @types/multer 2.1.0 (two units) were each already at one
exact version in every unit that declares them. Not one of them needed a
version to change. What kept them out of this file was which SECTION of
package.json they sat in: all three were in `dependencies`, and the checker
reports a wrong section as a misplacement rather than an absence, so a package
with a perfect version still fails.
That is the React problem again, and this block already records it: React was
unassertable through wave 4 because jewelry-factory kept @types/react in
`dependencies`. The fix then was one moved declaration plus a checker that
reads both sections. Nobody swept the rest of the fleet for the same defect at
the time, so it sat for seven waves.
@types/multer WAS NOT A CLEAN CONVERGENCE, and the difference is the finding.
jewelry-factory ran multer 2.2.0 against @types/multer 1.4.12 -- types a whole
major behind the library -- with tsc checking its upload routes against the
multer 1.x API surface and nothing red anywhere, because a wrong-major types
package fails silently by construction. expense-splitter ran the correct
pairing at 2.1.0, which is what made the target obvious rather than a
judgement call.
The bump found nothing. jewelry-factory's usage -- memoryStorage(),
upload.single(), req.file, Express.Multer.File -- sits in the part of the
surface that did not change across the major, so tsc is clean either way. The
defect was real and the consequence was nil, which is the expected shape of
this failure rather than a reason it did not matter: nothing was checking that
the code stayed inside the compatible subset, and nothing would have said so
when it stopped.
This is why @types/express is still NOT here while @types/multer now is. Both
are wrong-major types problems; only one is fixable. hiring-tracker runs
express 5.1.0 against the express 4 types while five units run express 4, so no
single asserted version is correct for all six and asserting one would fail the
correct fix (workflows#276). Every unit declaring @types/multer runs multer
2.x, so there is nothing to arbitrate.
WHAT THE WAVE 10 AND 11 SURVEYS ESTABLISHED TOGETHER, which is worth stating
as a rule rather than leaving in two issue threads: AGREEMENT IS NOT EVIDENCE
OF USE. Five packages have now been rejected from this file for sitting at one
version across units that do not consume them -- eslint-plugin-import and
eslint-plugin-react (workflows#274), @tailwindcss/vite (#275), and lodash,
which two repositories declared at 4.18.1 and neither imported anywhere. lodash
was deleted rather than asserted; in event-manager it was a SECOND copy of the
package, since jshint already pulls 4.17.21 through grunt, and in
hiring-tracker it was in `dependencies`, shipping in the production image for
code that never called it.
So a candidate needs two things, not one: every declaring unit at the same
exact version, AND at least one of them actually importing it. The first is
cheap to measure and the second is what the surveys kept getting wrong.
$dependencies_comment: Compared against package.json's `dependencies` -- RUNTIME packages, the
ones that ship. Same exactness rule as devDependencies above: a caret or
tilde is a failure.
The section is part of what is asserted, not incidental to it. A package
listed here must be in `dependencies` and a package listed above must be
in `devDependencies`, and the checker reports the wrong section as a
misplacement rather than as an absence. Placement is a real defect class
in both directions: a runtime package parked in devDependencies breaks a
--prod install, and a types package parked in dependencies ships nothing
but noise. Merging the two blocks into one lookup would assert the
versions and lose that.
react and react-dom converged in wave 4 of aurum-alpha/workflows#169.
They are one entry in two lines: react-dom peers an EXACT react version,
so they move together or the tree is wrong. @types/react-dom likewise
peers @types/react ^19.2.0, which is why both types sit above rather than
one of them.
A custom renderer is React-major-coupled whatever its peer range claims,
and that is worth knowing before the next React wave. react-konva@18.2.14
declares `react: >=18.0.0` -- which admits 19 and is a lie -- while
bundling react-reconciler ~0.29.0, React 18's. Only 19.2.5 bundles 0.33.0.
The peer range will not catch that; the resolved react-reconciler in the
lockfile is what proves the bump took.
